hypotheses.name: Currarino syndrome (anterior sacral meningocele)
hypotheses.rationale: Classic triad: presacral cystic mass, sacral bony defect (scimitar sacrum), and anorectal malformation (hypospadias/perineal opening). The MRI T2 hyperintensity and CT delayed enhancement are consistent with a meningocele.

hypotheses.name: Currarino syndrome (enteric cyst)
hypotheses.rationale: Enteric cysts are also common in Currarino syndrome but typically do not enhance with contrast unless infected or communicating.

hypotheses.name: Tailgut cyst
hypotheses.rationale: Can present as a presacral cyst but the sacral defect and anorectal malformation point to Currarino.

hypotheses.name: Teratoma
hypotheses.rationale: Presacral teratomas can occur but usually have mixed solid/cystic components and calcifications.

arguments.note: Evidence strongly supports Currarino syndrome triad: presacral cystic mass, scimitar sacrum, and anorectal malformation.

differential_diagnoses.name: Currarino syndrome (enteric cyst)
differential_diagnoses.why: Enteric cysts are also part of the Currarino triad but typically do not enhance with contrast. The delayed enhancement seen on CT favors meningocele.

differential_diagnoses.name: Tailgut cyst
differential_diagnoses.why: Can present as a presacral cyst but does not typically have the associated sacral defect and anorectal malformation seen here.

differential_diagnoses.name: Sacrococcygeal teratoma
differential_diagnoses.why: Presacral teratomas can occur but usually have mixed solid/cystic components and calcifications, which are not described here.

key_findings.fact: Severe hypospadias/perineal urethral opening with hypoplastic/bifid scrotum (anorectal malformation)
Large, well-defined, hyperintense cystic mass in the presacral/retrorectal space on MRI T2, compressing the rectum anteriorly
CT delayed phase shows the presacral cystic mass with high density suggesting contrast filling or thick enhancing wall
Scimitar sacrum (sacral bony defect in lower sacral segments) on CT bone window

uncertainty: The exact nature of the presacral mass (meningocele vs enteric cyst) cannot be definitively distinguished without surgical pathology, but the enhancement pattern favors meningocele.

differential_diagnoses.name: Presacral enteric cyst
differential_diagnoses.why: Enteric cysts are a component of the Currarino triad and present as presacral masses. However, they typically do not show contrast enhancement or filling, whereas the CT findings suggest contrast filling or a thick enhancing wall, making this less likely than a meningocele.

differential_diagnoses.name: Tailgut cyst (retrorectal cystic hamartoma)
differential_diagnoses.why: These are common presacral cysts in adults but are rare in children. They do not typically present with the specific sacral bony defect (scimitar sacrum) or anorectal malformations seen in this case.

differential_diagnoses.name: Sacrococcygeal teratoma
differential_diagnoses.why: While these are common presacral masses in neonates, they usually contain mixed solid and cystic components with calcifications. The imaging here describes a well-defined cystic mass without mention of calcification or solid elements.

key_findings.fact: Severe hypospadias/perineal urethral opening with hypoplastic/bifid scrotum
Large, well-defined, hyperintense cystic mass in the presacral/retrorectal space on MRI T2, compressing the rectum anteriorly
CT delayed phase shows high density in the presacral cystic mass, suggesting contrast filling or a thick enhancing wall
Scimitar sacrum (sacral bony defect in lower sacral segments) on CT bone window

uncertainty: While the enhancement pattern favors an anterior sacral meningocele over an enteric cyst, definitive histological confirmation would require surgical pathology.
